comment: Geography (AQA GCSE 8035) multiple choice for module 11, Paper 3: Issue Evaluation and Fieldwork. Covers the structure and marking of Paper 3, how the pre-release booklet works, the 2026 pre-release content (UK water supply and demand, the proposed Lincolnshire reservoir) as the worked example, John's two fieldwork enquiries (Brighton groynes, Stratford Olympic regeneration), the unseen-fieldwork question types, and the geographical skills in spec 3.4 — OS maps and grid references, presentation techniques, and statistics. Built from the Dulwich College Paper 3 Fieldwork Revision Workbook 2026, the Brighton and Stratford model answers, the Fieldwork Evaluation Summary, the Geography Pre-Release Booklet 2026 with its filled-in A3 evaluation grid and teaching slides, the AQA specification section 3.3-3.4, and the Paper 3 question papers, mark schemes and examiner's reports for 2019, 2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025. NOTE: this file still needs adding to the geography mcqBanks list in tools/subjects.js.

11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.q: How are the 76 marks on Paper 3 divided?
options: 38 marks for Section A and 38 for Section B
37 marks for Section A issue evaluation and 39 for Section B fieldwork
25 marks for Section A, 25 for Section B and 26 for skills
46 marks for Section A and 30 for Section B
11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.explain: Section A issue evaluation is 37 marks, Section B fieldwork is 39. The paper is 1 hour 15 minutes and 30% of the GCSE, with 6 of the 76 marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar.

11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.q: Where are the 6 SPaG marks on Paper 3 awarded?
options: Spread evenly across every question worth 4 marks or more
All six on the Section A decision question
On the two 6-mark discussion questions
Three on the Section A 9-marker and three on the Section B 9-marker
11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.explain: The front of the paper names exactly two questions for SPaG — the Section A 9-marker and the Section B familiar-fieldwork 9-marker — at 3 marks each. That is 6 of the 76, which is why paragraphing and geographical terminology matter on those two answers specifically.

11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.q: How long before the exam is the pre-release resources booklet issued, and what happens to your annotated copy?
options: Twelve weeks before; you take your annotated copy into the exam
Six weeks before; you memorise it because you get nothing in the exam
On the morning of the exam, with reading time
Twelve weeks before; you hand it back and get a clean copy in the exam
11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.explain: Twelve weeks (the 2026 booklet was issued on Thursday 19 March 2026). You work through and annotate it in class, but a clean, unmarked copy is issued in the exam room. That is why the twelve weeks are for annotating, categorising and ranking rather than memorising.

11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.q: A Section A answer that selects exactly the right sentence from the resources booklet and copies it across is marked at…
options: Level 3, because the evidence is appropriate
Level 2, because selecting evidence shows understanding
Level 1, because copying is not developing or evaluating
Zero, because quoting the booklet is not allowed
11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.explain: Every Paper 3 mark scheme says the same thing: copying is Level 1 even when the copied material is correct. Developing the point — 'this means that…' — reaches Level 2, and linking points from across the booklet to support a judgement reaches Level 3.

11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.q: Which assessment objective dominates Paper 3?
options: AO1, knowledge of locations, places and processes
AO2, understanding of geographical concepts
AO3, interpreting, analysing and evaluating information to make judgements
AO4 alone, the selection and use of skills
11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.explain: Paper 3 is nearly all AO3 with a substantial AO4 element — the 9-markers are marked AO3 6 / AO4 3. That is why the paper rewards judgement and skills rather than recall, and why the pre-release booklet can be in front of you without making the paper easy.

11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.q: In a Paper 3 Section A question that names no specific place, answering entirely through the booklet's case-study location is described by examiners as…
options: self-limiting, because the general question wants wider course understanding
the safest approach, because the resources are the only permitted evidence
worth full marks, as long as the detail is accurate
an automatic Level 1 cap
11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.explain: The 2023 report names this explicitly. Some questions tie to the location (the Cayman Islands questions) and some are broad topic discussions, where answers bringing in wider learning — economic leakage, seasonality, ecotourism — scored highest. Narrowing a general question to the location closes off marks without being wrong.

11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.q: In the 2026 pre-release booklet, which figure carries the specific proposed scheme and the stakeholders arguing about it?
options: Figure 1, water supply and demand in the UK
Figure 2, water futures
Figure 3, the proposed Lincolnshire reservoir
There is no such figure; the stakeholders are in the question paper
11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.explain: The three figures always do three jobs: Figure 1 the general problem with the national statistics, Figure 2 the possible solutions (plus the OS map of the site), Figure 3 the specific proposal with the stakeholder views. The 9-mark decision question is always set on Figure 3.

11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.q: What proportion of water supply in England comes from surface water?
11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.explain: Surface water is 64% of supply in England and 93% in Wales; the rest comes from groundwater, and England and Wales have 2259 groundwater sources against Scotland's 86. UK water companies supply over 16 billion litres a day in total.

11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.q: Of the projected increase in water demand in England between 2020 and 2050, how much falls in the South East?
11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.explain: The South East takes 50% of the increase, against the West 20%, Central and East 18%, and the North and South West 6% each. This is the key figure because the South East is also the driest region, receiving under 800 mm of rainfall a year — demand is growing fastest exactly where the resource is scarcest.

11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.q: Which single use accounts for the largest share of household water use in England?
options: Flushing toilets, at 30%
Personal washing, at 25%
Washing machines, at 21%
Garden use, at 7%
11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.explain: Toilets 30%, personal washing 25%, washing machines 21%, washing up 8%, garden 7%, drinking 4%, other 5%. Because flushing is the largest slice, rainwater harvesting into an underground tank used for flushing is the strongest single household measure.

11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.q: Roughly how much water is lost to leakage in England each day, and what share of supply is that?
options: Over 3 billion litres a day, about 20% of supply
140 to 150 million litres a day, about 2% of supply
16 billion litres a day, all of supply
4 billion litres a day, about 50% of supply
11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.explain: Over 3 billion litres a day, approximately 20% of supply. It is the residents' strongest argument against needing a new reservoir at all — the cheapest water available is water already treated and paid for. (140 to 150 million litres a day is the Thames desalination plant's output.)

11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.q: Serious water pollution incidents in England rose from 263 in 2020 to 325 in 2021. What is the percentage increase?
11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.explain: Percentage change divides by the ORIGINAL value: 62 ÷ 263 × 100 = 24%, the figure the booklet quotes. Dividing by the new value gives 19% and loses the mark — the commonest arithmetic error in this topic.

11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.q: How much water would the proposed Lincolnshire reservoir supply, and to how many homes?
options: 55 million litres a day to 175 000 homes
16 billion litres a day to the whole of eastern England
140 litres a day to 2000 homes
Up to 166 million litres a day to 500 000 homes
11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.explain: Up to 166 million litres a day to 500 000 homes, from a reservoir holding 55 million cubic metres. The 175 000 figure is the number of new homes planned in Lincolnshire over five years, and 140 litres a day is average personal consumption — don't mix them up.

11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.q: How would the proposed Lincolnshire reservoir be filled?
options: By desalinating water from the North Sea
By pumping groundwater from local aquifers all year round
By taking water from the Trent and Witham in winter when flows are highest
By rainwater harvesting across the catchment
11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.explain: Winter water is taken from the River Trent and River Witham when levels are highest, stored, then treated and supplied in the hotter summer months when river levels are low and demand is high. An overflow drain manages levels and reduces winter flood risk — which is why the scheme counts as climate-change adaptation.

11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.q: Which figure is the economic case for the Lincolnshire reservoir?
options: £2.6 billion of direct and indirect investment in the area
£55 million of government grant funding
2000 new permanent jobs on the reservoir
£166 million a year in water bills
11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.explain: £2.6 billion of direct and indirect investment, plus thousands of visitors a year using the sailing, wind surfing, cycling and walking facilities and spending with local businesses. The 2000 figure is the number of local people who signed the petition against the scheme.

11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.q: Why is the National Farmers Union's response the most useful single source in the 2026 booklet?
options: It is the only source with statistics in it
It opposes the scheme outright, so it supplies the whole negative case
It supports expanding water supply while warning about local harm, so it supplies both halves of a paragraph
It is written by the Environment Agency
11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.explain: The NFU fully supports expanding water infrastructure as a response to climate change and population growth, and says farms will benefit from the extra water — while warning that large-scale schemes significantly harm local farm businesses and communities and insisting local people be involved at every stage. A source on both sides gives you the evaluation for free.

11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.q: What is the title of John's physical geography fieldwork enquiry?
options: To what extent has the Olympic Regeneration of Stratford been successful?
Evaluate the success of groynes as a method of coastal management on Brighton beach
How does beach material change along the Brighton coastline?
Are sea walls more effective than groynes at Brighton?
11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.explain: The exact wording matters, because the examiners insist the answers must visibly reflect the aim in the title you write on the paper. The school's advice is to learn this enquiry for the 9-marker, because it is the more straightforward of the two to analyse.

11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.q: At what interval were the Brighton beach slope profiles measured, and what sampling method is that?
options: Every 1 m, random sampling
Every 5 m, stratified sampling
At three chosen spots, opportunity sampling
Every 2 m, systematic sampling
11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.explain: Every 2 m, measured from just above the breaking waves inland to the sea wall — systematic sampling, because the readings are taken at regular intervals. The justification is that 2 m gave enough detail of sediment build-up while staying quick enough to repeat on three adjacent groynes.

11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.q: Which four variables did the Brighton bi-polar analysis survey score?
options: Buildings, traffic, open space and general quality
Vulnerability to erosion, aesthetic value, lifespan, and disturbance to natural processes and habitats
Litter, vandalism, safety and green space
Width, height, gradient and sediment size
11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.explain: Those four, scored from -3 to +3, comparing the groynes with the sea wall. (Buildings, traffic, open space and general quality were the Stratford environmental quality survey's categories — a classic mix-up.)

11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.q: What did the Brighton slope profiles actually show?
options: More sediment on the downdrift (east) side and a deficit updrift
More sediment on the updrift (west) side and a clear deficit downdrift (east)
An equal amount of sediment either side of each groyne
No measurable difference, so the hypothesis was rejected
11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.explain: Longshore drift at Brighton runs west to east, so west is updrift. Sediment was trapped on the west side and depleted on the east, which is the evidence that the groynes are interrupting longshore drift and building a protective beach — the conclusion the title asked for.

11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.q: Which site scored highest in John's Stratford environmental quality survey, and with what score?
options: Site A, near Hackney Wick station, with +23
Site E, Westfield, with +17
Site C, East Village, with +31
Site B, the London Blossom Garden, with +23
11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.explain: Site B, the London Blossom Garden, at +23. Site A near Hackney Wick station scored lowest for building quality — it is peripheral to the park, grew from the 1990s with artists in converted warehouses, and has graffiti and more traffic. The contrast is the evidence that regeneration has been successful but uneven.

11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.q: What is the single biggest weakness of the Stratford questionnaire data?
options: The questions were all closed, so no qualitative data was collected
The sample was three people per site on one weekday, with no stratification by age
No one was willing to answer, so the sample was empty
It was collected in winter, so responses were unusually negative
11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.explain: Three people at each of five sites, one sunny weekday in the middle of the day — so residents were likely at work and tourists over-represented, and no age groups were deliberately sampled. Stratified sampling and a weekend visit would have fixed it. Q3 was an open question, so qualitative data was collected.

11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.q: How did John's class reduce the subjectivity of the Stratford environmental quality survey scores?
options: By taking a group average of the total score for each site, removing outliers
By using only one observer at every site
By discarding any site where scores disagreed
By converting the scores into percentages
11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.explain: A group average of totals removes the influence of outliers and improves accuracy and reliability. The other standard fix, from the fieldwork workbook, is a standardisation survey at one agreed point with everyone adjusting their scores to the group average before starting.

11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.q: 'Accurate', 'reliable' and 'valid' mean different things. Which set of definitions is right?
options: Accurate = repeatable; reliable = close to the true value; valid = officially approved
Accurate = quantitative; reliable = qualitative; valid = statistically significant
They are interchangeable terms for good data
Accurate = close to the true value; reliable = repeatable; valid = the conclusion is genuinely supported
11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.explain: Accuracy is about the measurement, reliability about repeatability, validity about the conclusion. The 2023 examiner's report found most candidates described their results or limitations but never linked them to the validity of the conclusion, and so stalled at Level 2 on the 9-marker. Write the chain: accuracy, therefore reliability, therefore validity.

11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.q: In a Section B question, 'suggest how the method could be ADAPTED' means…
options: suggest an additional data collection method, such as a questionnaire
change the method that is already shown in the figure
redesign the whole enquiry with a new hypothesis
explain why the method was chosen in the first place
11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.explain: The 2022 mark scheme explicitly refused credit for suggesting questionnaires on an 'adapt' question, because the answer had to reference the methods already in the figure. 'Additional' is the word that invites a new method — and in 2023 it also refused credit for repeating a question the figure had already asked.

11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.q: Which presentation technique is the right choice for investigating the relationship between two variables, such as river width and maximum depth?
options: A dispersion graph
An isoline map
A scattergraph
A pie chart
11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.explain: A scattergraph, with a line of best fit if you need to interpolate or extrapolate. A dispersion graph shows the spread of repeated readings at each site, an isoline map joins points of equal value, and a pie chart shows the composition of one whole. The 2023 report says only a very small proportion of candidates got the 'which technique' question right.

11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.q: On an OS map, what does the grid reference 1337 identify?
options: A point 100 m into the square, measured from the north-east corner
The square at easting 37, northing 13
The 1 km grid square whose south-west corner is easting 13, northing 37
A spot height of 1337 m
11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.explain: Eastings before northings — along the corridor, then up the stairs. Four figures name a whole 1 km square by its south-west corner; six figures divide that square into tenths and locate a point to 100 m. Each square is 1 km by 1 km, so it is also 1 km², which gives you distance and area for free.

11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.q: A question asks you to 'describe the physical geography' of an area on an OS map. What should the answer be about?
options: Roads, railways, settlements and named buildings
Relief and drainage — height, slope, rivers, lakes, ponds and woodland
The land uses shown in the key
The population density of the settlements
11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.explain: Relief and drainage. The 2022 examiner's report says very few candidates appeared to understand the term at all, and most wrote about human features. Level 1 is 'high land, low land and a river'; Level 2 needs precision — the slope, the height of the land, and the direction of flow of the rivers.

11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.q: Twelve areas score 4, 6, 6, 2, 9, 3, 10, 1, 5, 8, 10, 1 for housing quality. What is the best answer about the mode?
options: The mode is 1, because that is the lowest value
The mode is 10, because it appears most often
The data is trimodal — 1, 6 and 10 each appear twice — so the mode cannot usefully be calculated
The mode is 5.5, the same as the median
11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.explain: Exactly the point the 2019 mark scheme wanted: 'The mode cannot be calculated / trimodal / 1, 6, 10.' Saying so is creditworthy, not a failure. For the record, mean 5.41, median 5.5, range 9, interquartile range 6.

11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.q: Why might the interquartile range be more useful than the range, and when is no measure of central tendency much use at all?
options: The IQR describes the middle 50% so ignores extremes; and averages are little use when the enquiry is about differences between places
The IQR is easier to calculate; and averages are useless with fewer than ten readings
The IQR includes every value; and averages fail only when data is qualitative
The IQR is the same as the median; and averages are always the best measure
11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.explain: The range is set entirely by the two most extreme readings, while the IQR (upper quartile minus lower quartile) describes the spread of the middle 50% — which is why the 2019 mark scheme offers it as a better alternative. The deeper point from that mark scheme: measures of central tendency 'have limited use… since it is really about identifying differences and patterns' — collapsing twelve areas into one number destroys what the enquiry set out to find.
